summary: Lays out a framework for delivering Internet Media Guides, which are collections of multimedia session descriptions written in SDP or a similar format. It describes a general model for delivery mechanisms, how existing protocols fit, and where new work is needed. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Like a TV guide for the Internet, listing what shows are on and how to tune in. This paper explains how such a guide could be handed out to everyone.

questions: what is an internet media guide
multicast vs unicast in img systems
subtitle: A framework for delivering multimedia session descriptions to large audiences.

tldr.problem: Broadcasting multimedia services requires a way to describe what is available and deliver that information to a potentially very large audience efficiently, over diverse network topologies. There is no single framework for how different protocols should coordinate these deliveries.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a common framework with three parts: data types (complete descriptions, delta updates, and pointers), operations (announce, query, subscribe, notify), and roles (senders, receivers, and intermediate nodes that may modify metadata). Existing protocols like SIP, HTTP, and SAP can be mapped to these operations.
tldr.outcome: The framework organizes how metadata should flow and which protocols suit which scenarios. However, the RFC also identifies gaps where new protocols and additional specifications are still needed for multicast, unicast, and envelope formats.

facts.value: Unidirectional multicast, bidirectional unicast, intermediary relay

today: RFC 4435 is an Informational RFC published in April 2006. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and serves as the foundational framework document for IMG delivery. However, the gaps it identified—particularly the need for a new multicast transport protocol and standardized envelope format—have not been fully addressed by subsequent RFCs, leaving IMG as a framework without complete end-to-end specifications.

sections.title: What Internet Media Guides Are
sections.content:
An Internet Media Guide (IMG) is a structured collection of metadata describing multimedia services and sessions. For example, it might list available TV programs, their schedules, how to access them, and their properties. The metadata is expressed using standard formats such as SDP (Session Description Protocol) or MPEG-7.

The fundamental challenge is distributing IMG metadata efficiently to potentially millions of receivers over diverse network topologies. Some receivers may have multicast access, others only unicast. Some may want unsolicited announcements like a traditional broadcast, while others prefer to query and retrieve metadata on demand. The RFC provides a unified framework that explains how to handle all these scenarios.
sections.eli5: An IMG is like a digital TV guide listing programs. The hard part is delivering it to everyone in different ways: by broadcast, by request, or by subscription. This RFC explains how to make all those delivery methods work together.

sections.title: The Core Framework
sections.content:
The framework has three core elements. First, data types: a Complete IMG Description is a self-contained set of metadata for one service; a Delta IMG Description is a partial update describing only changes; an IMG Pointer identifies or references metadata without including the metadata itself.

Second, IMG operations: IMG ANNOUNCE sends unsolicited metadata to one or more receivers; IMG QUERY asks for metadata; IMG RESOLVE answers a query; IMG SUBSCRIBE registers to receive updates; IMG NOTIFY sends updates to subscribers. These operations cover the major message patterns: one-way broadcast, request-reply, and subscription-based events.

Third, IMG entities: An IMG Sender originates metadata (via Announcer, Resolver, or Notifier roles). An IMG Receiver consumes metadata (via Listener, Querier, or Subscriber roles). An IMG Transceiver is both sender and receiver, and may modify, aggregate, or filter metadata as it passes through.
sections.eli5: IMGs have three parts: the metadata itself (full or updated), the operations (tell everyone, answer a question, or send updates), and the roles (who sends, who receives, and who relays). This lets any server or device handle IMG messages in many different ways.

sections.title: How It Is Delivered
sections.content:
IMG metadata can be delivered in four broad patterns. In one-to-many unidirectional multicast, one sender broadcasts announcements to many receivers with no uplink needed; receivers just listen. In one-to-one bidirectional unicast, a receiver queries a sender or subscribes to updates over a reliable connection; the sender responds or sends notifications as data changes.

An intermediary (transceiver) receives metadata from one or more senders, possibly modifies or aggregates it (for example, a rating service might add ratings to program metadata), and forwards it to receivers. This pattern is important because metadata often needs to be localized or enriched before reaching the end user. One drawback: if an intermediary modifies metadata, the original digital signature becomes invalid.

A combined system may use multiple protocols for different operations all sharing the same metadata, so that some receivers listen for announcements while others query on demand or subscribe, all retrieving consistent information from the same source.
sections.eli5: IMG metadata flows in different ways: some receivers tune in and listen passively, others ask for specific shows, and some sign up to be notified of changes. Sometimes a relay station modifies the metadata before passing it on. All these patterns can coexist.

sections.title: Applying Existing Protocols
sections.content:
Many existing protocols can be adapted to IMG operations. SDP and SDPng describe session parameters and fit into Complete IMG Descriptions. MPEG-7 and TV-Anytime provide detailed metadata about content, schedules, and user preferences. HTTP works for query-reply (IMG QUERY and RESOLVE) but does not naturally support server-initiated notifications, so subscriptions would require polling.

SAP (Session Announcement Protocol) supports multicast announcement but has severe limitations: it lacks scalability, reliability, extensibility, and payload segmentation. SIP event subscriptions enable IMG SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY over unicast but lack multicast support. RTSP has methods similar to IMG operations but they are tied to streaming control and cannot be used independently.

The framework shows that most existing protocols cover pieces of the problem, but none fully address all IMG scenarios. Notably, there is no adequate open standard for reliable multicast announcements, which is critical for unidirectional broadcast scenarios.
sections.eli5: Some protocols can carry parts of IMG metadata: SDP describes what is on, HTTP lets you ask for details, SIP lets servers push updates. But nothing covers everything, especially reliable multicast broadcast to huge audiences.

sections.title: What Still Needs to Be Specified
sections.content:
The RFC identifies four major gaps. First, a multicast transport protocol for announcements is needed: reliable, extensible, able to handle large payloads with congestion control. The RFC recommends building on ALC (Asynchronous Layered Coding) or FLUTE (File Delivery over Unidirectional Transport), existing multicast protocols designed for the job.

Second, a specification for using existing unicast protocols like HTTP, SIP, and SIP events for IMG operations is needed. Third, an IMG envelope is required: a standard way to wrap metadata with version numbers, expiry times, and globally unique identifiers, independent of the metadata format itself. Options include embedding in transport headers, wrapping with a separate envelope object, or wrapping metadata in XML.

Fourth, standardized metadata data models are needed so different applications can interoperate, extending and reusing metadata definitions consistently. These specifications are beyond the scope of this framework but are essential to actual deployment.
sections.eli5: To make IMGs work, four things are still missing: a reliable way to broadcast to millions, standard rules for using normal unicast protocols, a common label format for all metadata, and agreements on what information different types of guides should contain.

sections.title: Security and Practical Concerns
sections.content:
The RFC notes several security issues without mandating specific solutions, since IMG is a framework and specific protocols will provide their own security. Privacy concerns arise when metadata reveals user habits or preferences; standard confidentiality protections apply. IMG authenticity is important: receivers should be assured of the origin and unmodified state of metadata to prevent hijacking or denial-of-service attacks.

Intermediaries present a trade-off: they enable aggregation and localization but break end-to-end authentication. Fragment-level signing might allow intermediaries to change some parts while preserving signatures on others. Authorization may be needed so private metadata is restricted to authorized receivers. Unidirectional links complicate security since many security protocols assume bidirectional communication.

The RFC also warns against allowing IMG operations to execute code or have write access to critical system areas, and notes that while executable code is not envisioned for IMG, some transport protocols might be capable of delivering arbitrary files.
sections.eli5: IMG metadata can leak your watching habits, so privacy matters. Receivers need to know metadata is real and not faked. Intermediaries that change metadata can break the proof of authenticity. Careful design is needed so metadata operators cannot harm the system.
